title: They only point (273–276)
hookLine: of paths the eightfold is best; you yourself must make the effort; the Buddhas only show the way

lines: THEY CAN'T WALK IT FOR YOU.
cards: You're lost in a strange city, and you ask someone for directions. They're wonderful.

They draw a little map on a napkin, name the landmarks, even walk you to the corner and point: three blocks that way, then left at the bakery. Then they go back to their day, because that's all anyone can do.
They can't walk the three blocks for you. Stand on the corner admiring the napkin, and you'll never get there.
Chapter twenty of the Dhammapada is called the way, and one of its verses says, very plainly, what even a Buddha can and can't do.

teach.h: THE EIGHTFOLD WAY, THE FOUR WORDS.
teach.b: The chapter opens with a list of bests.

Verse two seventy-three, in Max Müller's translation: "The best of ways is the eightfold; the best of truths the four words; the best of virtues passionlessness; the best of men he who has eyes to see."
The eightfold way is the path this course has met before: right view, intention, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness and concentration. The four words are the four noble truths.

teach.h: YOU YOURSELF MUST MAKE AN EFFORT.
teach.b: Then, after urging the listener onto the way, comes verse two seventy-six, the heart of today: "You yourself must make an effort. The Tathagatas (Buddhas) are only preachers."
Tathāgata is one of the Buddha's own titles, the thus-gone one.
The Pali for only preachers is akkhātāro: the ones who tell, who declare, who point out. The verse never promises that the Tathagatas walk the way for anyone.

The Buddha, in this verse, is the person on the corner pointing down the street. The walking is yours. The Pali word for effort here is ātappa, from a root meaning heat: the warmth of steady, ardent work.
Later Buddhist traditions, especially Chan and Zen, loved a related image: the teaching is a finger pointing at the moon. Don't stare at the finger.

teach.h: A FINGER, A RAFT, YOUR FEET.
teach.b: And in an early discourse, the Buddha compares the teaching to a raft, for crossing a river, not for carrying on your head once you're across.
The images differ, but the point is the same: a teacher shows the way. Your feet make the journey.

how: Buddhists revere the Buddha as the teacher who found and showed the path, while holding that each person must walk it through their own effort; the eightfold path and four noble truths are taught across Buddhist schools.

games.q: someone has drawn you a perfect map and pointed you down the right street. what does verse 276 say comes next?
o: wait for them to walk you there.
frame the map and admire it.
games.why: "you yourself must make an effort." even the Buddhas only point the way.

practice: Picture whatever is pointing for you, a teacher, a verse, even this lesson, and notice where it points: toward this breath, this body, this moment.

Then take one step: put your whole attention on a single breath, from its first cool edge in the nostrils to the last of the out-breath, and then another. Nobody else can take it for you, and nobody needs to.

orig.note: Pali: path, way — chapter twenty is the Maggavagga; the eightfold path is the ariya aṭṭhaṅgika magga.

carryVoice: Your line: your feet make the journey. Directions are not the walk itself. Until tomorrow.
